questions.q: What are the three categories into which Belsky sorts project tasks?
a: Action steps, references and backburner items
Urgent tasks, important tasks and optional tasks
Creative work, admin work and client work
Daily tasks, weekly tasks and monthly tasks
questions.why: Lesson 1 divides every project into action steps, reference material and nice-to-have backburner items.

questions.q: How does the summary describe a “dreamer”?
a: Someone full of ideas who struggles to see one through
Someone who finishes projects but resists new ideas
Someone who balances ideas and execution perfectly
Someone who avoids creative work and focuses on numbers
questions.why: Lesson 2 defines dreamers as idea-rich but weak on follow-through, unlike doers and incrementalists.

questions.q: Why is it useful to know whether you are a dreamer, doer or incrementalist?
a: You can partner with people whose strengths complement yours
You can avoid ever working with people of the same type
You can choose a career that requires no collaboration
You can eliminate the weaknesses of your own type
questions.why: Lesson 2 says knowing your type lets you find partners who fill the gaps, so you go further together.

A list of tasks sorted by how much energy they have already cost
A schedule that places your hardest work early in the day
A measure of how energized you feel after each project
questions.why: Lesson 3 defines it as projects sorted by future energy and value, setting aside sunk costs.

questions.q: What mistake does the summary say people make when choosing which project to work on?
a: They judge by effort already spent rather than future value
They always pick the newest project on their desk
They ask clients to decide the priority for them
They refuse to work on more than one project at a time
questions.why: Lesson 3 warns against deciding based on past investment instead of the project’s strategic and economic value.
